title: Sysmon CreateRemoteThread Between Processes
exclusions: Reports each Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 8 where a process creates a thread in another process. It does not detect every process-injection technique, prove memory was allocated/written, prove the new thread executed malicious code, identify a loaded payload, establish privilege escalation/credential theft, or replace EDR/memory forensics. Event ID 10 means one process opened another and its GrantedAccess is an access mask; this UC does not relabel selected masks as confirmed memory writes or hollowing. Event ID 25 process tampering, Event ID 7 image load, and Event ID 1 process creation are separate context. Sysmon infers StartModule and StartFunction and Microsoft says they may be empty. SourceUser/TargetUser can be inconsistent, so both raw fields are preserved. The one-event trigger, five-minute cadence/allowance, severity, retention, and exceptions are local choices. The rule performs no kill, isolation, blocking, or compliance attestation.
evidence: After deployment, retain the qualified Sysmon binary/configuration/hash and Event ID 16 changes; effective Event ID 8 XML input and Splunk Add-on for Sysmon version; endpoint/source/field health; approved source-target baseline; `windows_sysmon_create_remote_thread` saved-search definition/ACL/schedule/dispatch; each result and raw XML; correlated Event IDs 1/7/10/25, EDR handle/memory/thread/module, file/signature/hash, logon, network, software/change, and forensic evidence; disposition; exact bounded exception; and dated positive, empty-inferred-field, wrong-event, duplicate, delayed, boundary, field-loss, and recovery tests. This documentation-only review created no remote thread/event, changed no Sysmon configuration, and executed no search, alert, dashboard, or response.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index and fixed dispatch slice, replay authentic-shaped Sysmon XML EventCode 8 with SourceImage `C:\Lab\uc12124-source.exe`, TargetImage `C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exe`, distinct source/target ProcessGuid and ProcessId, SourceUser/TargetUser, NewThreadId, StartAddress, StartModule `-`, StartFunction `-`, EventRecordID, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Expect exactly one `create_remote_thread` row preserving source/target identities and explicit `unknown` inferred module/function, with `use_case=UC-1.2.124`. Repeat with populated StartModule/StartFunction and expect those values unchanged.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Replay Sysmon EventCodes 1, 7, 10, and 25 carrying similar source/target fields, EventCode 8 from a wrong source/type/provider, and an EventCode 8 outside the completed slice; expect zero rows. Replay an EventCode 8 missing SourceImage, TargetImage, or EventRecordID and expect a retained row with `unknown` plus a field-quality finding rather than silent suppression. Prove duplicate direct/WEC copies are reported by source health, and prove an exact unexpired endpoint/source-hash/target/start tuple exception suppresses delivery only after the base row; expired, process-name-only, wildcard, or source-health exceptions must not hide evidence.

dataSources: Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 8 (`CreateRemoteThread`) from `Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Sysmon > Operational`, collected in XML to deployment-chosen `index=windows`, `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` with Splunk Add-on for Sysmon. Required fields are `_time`, `_indextime`, `Computer`/`host`, source/type/provider, `EventCode`, `EventRecordID`, `SourceProcessGuid`, `SourceProcessId`, `SourceImage`, `TargetProcessGuid`, `TargetProcessId`, `TargetImage`, `NewThreadId`, `StartAddress`, `StartModule`, `StartFunction`, `SourceUser`, and `TargetUser`. Event IDs 1, 7, 10, and 25 plus EDR/memory evidence are optional corroboration, not merged into the base fact.
app: Splunk Add-on for Sysmon (`Splunk_TA_microsoft_sysmon`, Splunkbase 5709) 5.0.1 supplies the supported Sysmon input and Event ID 8 field extractions for Splunk Platform 9.2+ and Sysmon 15.0. A deployment app supplies source health, the raw saved search, exact source-target baseline/exception, fixtures, dashboard, and runbook. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=windows sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=8 earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval endpoint=lower(trim(coalesce(Computer,dvc,dest,host))), source_process_guid=coalesce(SourceProcessGuid,parent_process_guid,"unknown"), source_process_id=coalesce(SourceProcessId,parent_process_id,"unknown"), source_image=coalesce(SourceImage,parent_process_path,"unknown"), target_process_guid=coalesce(TargetProcessGuid,process_guid,"unknown"), target_process_id=coalesce(TargetProcessId,process_id,"unknown"), target_image=coalesce(TargetImage,process_path,"unknown"), source_user=coalesce(SourceUser,"unknown"), target_user=coalesce(TargetUser,"unknown"), new_thread_id=coalesce(NewThreadId,"unknown"), start_address=coalesce(StartAddress,src_address,"unknown"), start_module=if(isnull(StartModule) OR StartModule="" OR StartModule="-","unknown",StartModule), start_function=if(isnull(StartFunction) OR StartFunction="" OR StartFunction="-","unknown",StartFunction), event_record_id=coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber,"unknown")
| where len(endpoint)>0
| eval action="create_remote_thread", event_time=strftime(_time,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), indexed_time=strftime(_indextime,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), use_case="UC-1.2.124"
| table _time event_time indexed_time endpoint action source_image source_process_guid source_process_id source_user target_image target_process_guid target_process_id target_user new_thread_id start_address start_module start_function event_record_id source sourcetype use_case
| sort 0 -_time endpoint source_image target_image
description: Detects each Sysmon Event ID 8 CreateRemoteThread observation in the completed dispatch slice and preserves source process, target process, users, new thread, start address, inferred module/function, record identity, and event/index times. Empty inferred fields remain `unknown`; the row describes remote-thread creation rather than declaring arbitrary process injection or malware.
value: Creating a thread in another live process is a high-signal execution primitive used by legitimate instrumentation and by malware to run under a different process context. Complete source-target-start evidence accelerates process-lineage, memory, module, and software-owner investigation while avoiding unsafe exclusions and unsupported claims that a ProcessAccess mask or one remote thread proves compromise.
implementation: Deploy and qualify Sysmon 15.0 with Event ID 8 included, collect its Operational channel as XML through Splunk Add-on for Sysmon 5.0.1, and verify every source/target/thread/start field against raw XML. Save `windows_sysmon_create_remote_thread`, run every five minutes over the preceding complete five-minute slice after five minutes of measured ingestion allowance, and trigger on any result. Enrich with hashes/signers and correlate Events 1/7/10/25 plus EDR/memory evidence before severity or response; apply only exact expiring notification exceptions after retaining the base row.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — CreateRemoteThread`: lead with expected-endpoint Sysmon/Event-8/source health, configuration drift, duplicate routes, and missing source/target/start fields. Show a newest-first source→target table, 24-hour timeline, 30-day source-target-start-module prevalence, high-value target panel, unknown StartModule/Function rate, source/target signer/hash enrichment, and raw XML/process-tree drilldown. Never render `unknown` inference as malicious shellcode or no rows as no injection activity.
schema: Native Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 8 CreateRemoteThread XML with Splunk Add-on for Sysmon aliases
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the primary detector. The Sysmon add-on exposes normalized process/parent/start fields for Event ID 8, but a generic Endpoint.Processes count does not guarantee source-versus-target GUID/PID/path, SourceUser/TargetUser, NewThreadId, StartAddress, inferred module/function, EventRecordID, or raw XML. Add summary acceleration only after exact parity and source-health tests; the raw Event ID 8 record remains authoritative.

knownFalsePositives:
A returned row is a genuine Sysmon CreateRemoteThread observation; the false positive is classifying every legitimate cross-process thread as malicious injection.

1. **Endpoint security, EDR, antivirus, anti-cheat, or application-control sensor** — Security products can instrument or inspect processes. Require exact source and target paths/hashes/signers, product/version, service, StartAddress/Module/Function pattern, endpoint role, deployment inventory, and owner. Do not globally suppress vendor names or every signed binary.

2. **Debugger, profiler, accessibility, automation, or UI testing tool** — Approved engineering/support software can create remote threads. Match tool hash/version, operator/session, target process, ticket/project, lab/production scope, exclusive UTC window, and expected start routine. Developer-tool presence alone is insufficient.

3. **Crash handling and console control behavior** — Windows components can produce expected remote-thread patterns such as control routines, including cases with unknown source process. Validate exact Windows build, source/target identity, StartAddress/Module/Function, users, event pattern, and adjacent process events. Never hard-code all `csrss`, `wermgr`, `KERNELBASE!CtrlRoutine`, or unknown sources as safe across builds.

4. **Application monitoring, APM, RPA, remote support, overlay, or input method software** — These products can inject helper threads into managed applications. Confirm approved package/hash/version, target set, business owner, expected module/function, deployment/change record, and prevalence.

5. **Backup, forensics, dump, migration, or support collection** — Privileged tools may instrument another process during a bounded job. Match exact case/job, source/target, operator/service, process hashes, start routine, endpoint set, and time; a generic maintenance window is not sufficient.

6. **Authorized red-team or control test** — Match exercise ID, named operator, exact endpoint/source hash/target/start tuple, exclusive interval, expected Event 8 and correlated EDR evidence, and cleanup. Preserve base row and alert evidence.

7. **Duplicate direct/WEC collection or replay** — Compare Computer, channel, EventRecordID, raw hash, and `_indextime`. Repair collection/checkpoint overlap; do not deduplicate by source-target because repeated threads can be real.

**Safe notification suppression:** apply lookup windows_create_remote_thread_exceptions.csv after the base row, keyed by exact lowercase endpoint or governed asset group, source path/hash/signer, target path/hash, StartModule/StartFunction or validated address pattern, product/version/job, numeric `valid_from`/exclusive `valid_until`, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject process-name-only, broad Windows/System32/vendor, wildcard, open-ended, unknown-field, and source-health exceptions. Preserve the original event and matched exception.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 8/10/25 and tuning documentation, current Splunk Sysmon add-on field mappings and Security Content, and MITRE ATT&CK process-injection behavior-chain guidance; no Sysmon configuration, remote-thread generation, XML field extraction, SPL execution, source-target baseline, fixture replay, EDR/memory correlation, exception, alert, dashboard, response, or Microsoft/Splunk/endpoint-security SME runtime sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: The scheduled search selects one typically low-volume Sysmon Event ID over one completed five-minute slice. Shared endpoint/index storage depends on the full Sysmon configuration; EDR/process-access correlation and retained raw XML add investigative cost.
sources: Microsoft Sysmon Operational XML Event ID 8
Optional Sysmon Events 1, 7, 10, and 25 plus EDR evidence

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact event contract

Assign endpoint-security, Sysmon configuration, Splunk collection/content, EDR/forensics, application-owner, source-health, and incident-response roles. Inventory in-scope endpoints/roles, Windows/Sysmon version, active configuration/hash, direct versus WEF/WEC route, expected security/debug/profiling/instrumentation tools, and owners. Install Sysmon 15.0 and Splunk Add-on for Sysmon 5.0.1 through controlled deployment; qualify exact endpoint, forwarder, add-on, indexer, search-head, and Splunk Cloud versions.

Microsoft defines Event ID 8 narrowly: a process created a thread in another process. SourceImage/Guid/Id and TargetImage/Guid/Id identify the pair; NewThreadId and StartAddress identify the thread start; StartModule and StartFunction are inferred and may be empty outside known loaded modules/exports. SourceUser/TargetUser were added in later Sysmon schemas and the Splunk add-on documents consistency limitations. Preserve both rather than collapsing them into one user.

One Event ID 8 produces one result. It is a strong process-modification signal but not proof that preceding memory allocation/write, malicious payload, successful execution, or privilege escalation occurred. MITRE's behavior-chain guidance combines process access/memory/thread/module/process activity. This UC deliberately avoids promising all process-injection coverage.

## Step 1 — Configure and collect Event ID 8

Merge a reviewed `CreateRemoteThread` include into the organization's Sysmon XML. Start with visibility on a representative cohort and tune after observing exact source-target-start tuples; avoid copying internet exclusions that discard all Windows, AV, or EDR processes. Record active configuration hash, verify Event ID 16 on changes, and inspect Event ID 255 errors. Confirm **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Sysmon > Operational** locally.

Collect XML through an app-owned input:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = windows
checkpointInterval = 5
```

The add-on documents `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`; channel identity is `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational`. Do not edit `default`. For WEF/WEC, use dedicated collector guidance, preserve originating Computer, measure subscription latency, and prevent simultaneous local plus collector ingestion. Restrict raw paths/users/addresses and correlated memory evidence.

Inspect Event ID 8 raw XML across qualified Windows/Sysmon builds. Verify every required field and aliases. Specifically test `-`, empty, and populated StartModule/StartFunction; differing SourceUser/TargetUser; unknown source process; process termination before ingestion; and hexadecimal addresses. Do not infer shellcode from an unknown module/function.

## Step 2 — Establish source and field health

Maintain expected endpoint/config/route/owner inventory. Health searches must detect no recurring Sysmon telemetry, active-config drift, Event ID 255 errors, wrong source/type/provider/channel, missing source or target GUID/path, missing EventRecordID, invalid thread/address, inference-null rate, duplicate Computer/channel/EventRecordID, excessive `_indextime-_time`, clock skew, forwarder/WEC queue, and add-on drift. Event ID 8 may be rare, so use recurring Sysmon/deployment telemetry as heartbeat; no Event 8 is not proof of no injection.

Build a versioned baseline from exact source/target path and hash/signer, source/target user, StartModule/Function/address pattern, endpoint role/build, software/product/version, service/job, cadence, and owner. Baseline distinct Windows builds and security agents. Keep rare/unseen as review context, not automatic maliciousness. Ingestion filters require security-owner review, before/after volume/coverage tests, rollback, and retained source health.

## Step 3 — Save and understand the SPL

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_sysmon_create_remote_thread`. Schedule every five minutes with `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`, evaluating one complete five-minute slice after five minutes of indexing allowance. Measure p99 direct/WEC delay and adjust schedule plus controls if inadequate. Trigger on any row; group delivery only on exact endpoint, source GUID, target GUID, thread ID/record ID, and bounded time.

The base clause fixes index, XML source type, exact Sysmon channel, EventCode, and closed window. Coalescing supports qualified raw/add-on aliases while retaining `unknown`. Source and target concepts remain separate. `-`, empty, or null inferred module/function becomes `unknown` so dashboards do not mistake a dash for a named module. Output preserves record and event/index times.

Do not append Event ID 10 rows into the same unlabeled table. Microsoft says Event 10 means one process opened another; it can precede queries, reads, or writes and can be noisy. Access values such as `0x1fffff`, `0x801`, or `0x1ffb` are masks whose rights depend on the bit set and platform; none alone proves WriteProcessMemory or process hollowing. Correlate Event 10 source/target GUID and time downstream with explicit mask decoding and tests. Event 25 directly reports supported process-tampering classes and also deserves separate semantics.

Do not hard-exclude `csrss`, `MsMpEng`, `SentinelAgent`, `CrowdStrike`, or `lsass` by substring. Filenames can be spoofed, products change, and targets can be sensitive. Use exact hash/version/source-target/start tuples in post-result baseline/notification handling.

## Step 4 — Validate semantics, timing, duplicates, and scale

Use authentic-shaped XML from the qualified Sysmon/add-on pair and fixed dispatch times. Run both controls. Add cases for populated/empty/dash inferred fields, same-user/different-user, unknown source image, Unicode paths, long paths, PID reuse, multiple threads, same source-target but distinct thread/record IDs, missing required fields, wrong source/provider/type/index, Event IDs 1/7/10/25, and exact earliest/latest boundaries.

Generate a remote-thread event only on a disposable isolated endpoint with an approved benign test harness or accountable detection framework. Target a harmless lab process; do not inject unreviewed shellcode, access credentials, or test on production. Compare Event Viewer **Details > XML View**, raw Splunk event, search output, process hashes/signers, EDR thread/memory telemetry, and the harness's expected source/target/start routine. Remove test artifacts and preserve exact versions, commands, hashes, times, record IDs, and expected/actual output.

Test direct/WEC duplicates, checkpoint reset, delayed events, source/target termination, configuration change, Event ID 255, forwarder/collector restart, clock skew, high security-agent activity, dashboard cardinality, alert delivery, and recovery. Test exact exception, changed hash/target/start/version, expiry boundary, malformed rows, wildcard rejection, retained evidence, and source-health independence. Keep draft until source health, fields, baseline, fixtures, alert, dashboard, exceptions, and response are accepted.

## Step 5 — Investigate and respond with corroboration

Alert text should state `CreateRemoteThread observed: <source> → <target> on <endpoint>`, not `injection confirmed`. Include source/target GUID/PID/path/user, hashes/signers/parents from enrichment, thread ID, start address/module/function with inference caveat, event/index time, record ID, endpoint role, prevalence, software/change, exception, and runbook.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify raw Event 8, source metadata, source/target/thread/record identity, inferred fields, time/latency, source health, and duplicates.
2. Correlate both ProcessGuid values with Event ID 1/EDR process creation, parent/command line, signer/hash, file provenance, user/logon, service/task, integrity/protection level, and endpoint role.
3. Inspect preceding Event ID 10/EDR process handles and decode access rights; seek validated memory allocation/write/API evidence, not mask folklore.
4. Inspect Event ID 7/EDR module loads, target thread/start mapping, memory-region protection/content, subsequent target activity/children/network/files, and Event ID 25 tampering.
5. Compare exact tuple with EDR/AV, debugger/profiler, accessibility, APM/RPA, remote support, crash handling, backup/forensic software, and approved change.
6. If suspicious, follow approved endpoint containment and memory/evidence acquisition. If authorized, document exact product/version/tuple and add only a bounded exception.
7. Confirm source/target disposition, no unexpected recurrence/follow-on, source health, exception expiry, and retained evidence.

Never terminate source/target, dump memory, isolate, or block automatically from one event. Some legitimate products rely on cross-process threads, and killing security/system software can destabilize the host. Review baselines/exceptions after Windows, Sysmon, EDR, AV, debugger, APM, remote-support, WEC, or add-on changes.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot product-specific failures

- **No Event ID 8:** verify Sysmon service/version, active CreateRemoteThread rules/schema, Event IDs 16/255, local channel, input deployment, WEC/forwarder queues, index/RBAC, and dispatch time.
- **StartModule/Function empty:** Microsoft says they are inferred and may be empty outside loaded modules/exports. Preserve StartAddress and correlate EDR/memory/module evidence; do not suppress or call it shellcode automatically.
- **SourceImage unknown:** inspect process lifetime and adjacent Event ID 1/5, source GUID/PID/time, EDR, and known console-control behavior. Track field quality and never allow-list unknown globally.
- **SourceUser and TargetUser differ unexpectedly:** preserve both; the add-on documents Sysmon user-field inconsistencies. Validate raw XML, event/schema/add-on version, logon/process context, and do not force one CIM user.
- **Event 10 appears without Event 8:** ProcessAccess has broader semantics and many injection techniques do not create a remote thread. Investigate under its own tuned contract; do not manufacture an Event 8.
- **Duplicates:** compare Computer/channel/EventRecordID/raw hash/index time and direct/WEC/checkpoint routes. Repair collection; repeated distinct thread IDs are not duplicates.
- **Security product flood:** verify exact signed hashes/versions/source-target-start tuples and product owner before an expiring exception. Avoid ingestion-wide vendor exclusions.
- **Dashboard says process injection:** correct the label to CreateRemoteThread observation and preserve evidence limits; one event is not a verdict.
grandmaExplanation: We watch when one Windows program starts a new thread inside another program. That can be normal security or support software, or a way to hide harmful code, so the team checks both programs and the memory evidence before deciding.
hardware: Windows clients and servers with Microsoft Sysmon 15.0 installed/running, CreateRemoteThread Event ID 8 included in the active configuration, and XML collection. Other injection primitives, kernel activity, protected-process limitations, endpoints without Sysmon, and activity predating retention require EDR or forensic telemetry.
